176:
## 12. Jhānavibhaṅga (Analysis of Jhāna)
## 1. Suttantabhājanīya (Suttanta Classification)
## Mātikāvaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Matrix)
Accomplishment of the preliminary duties (pubbabhāgakaraṇīyasampadā) of jhāna refers to practices such as the restraint of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkhasaṃvara-sīla). Since jhāna on the foul (asubha-jhāna), jhāna on the recollections (anussati-jhāna), and supramundane jhāna (lokuttara-jhāna) do not exist outside this Dispensation (Sāsana), the phrase "in every way" (sabbappakārena) is used to include them all. By the statement, "Other doctrines are empty of recluses," it is shown that even a person accomplished in the preliminary duties that lead to recluseship does not exist outside the Dispensation. Regarding the training rules (sikkhāpadesu) which are taught by way of the mental body (nāmakāya) etc., and which should be practiced by not transgressing the word, or in the sense of the collection of trainings consisting of the volition of restraint (virati-cetanā) that should be fulfilled without transgression—those various trainings such as the bhikkhu-training are parts of the training rules and should be practiced. Thus, it is said that the word "sikkhāpadesu" is an exposition of the states that should be trained in.

In relation to contentment (santoṣa) etc., the following virtues are shown: being satisfied with whatever requisites are obtained, praising the virtue of such contentment, not longing for requisites when they are not obtained, and consuming them without greed when they are obtained. The description of the one who performs the jhāna-meditation is an exposition of the state of being a performer (kārakabhāvapari dīpana). By the word "forest" etc., the types of lodgings (senāsana) are shown; by the word "little noise" etc., the state of being free from faults is shown; and by the word "suitable for seclusion," the benefits (ānisaṃsa) are shown. Thus, it is said, "The types of lodgings... exposition."

## Mātikāvaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā (The Explanation of the Matrix is Finished).

## Niddesavaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Exposition)
Because the Dispensation is taught using the word "diṭṭhi" (view) in the sense of an object (kamma-attha), it is said, "It is called diṭṭhi because it is seen," and so on. "Sabhāvaṭṭhena" means in the sense of reality (non-perversion). Only the discipline (vinaya) that is being trained in can discipline the body and so on, and not by any other means; thus it is said, "It is called vinaya in the sense of that which should be trained in." Or else, vinaya is...
177:
The training rules (sikkhāpada) that should be trained in, and the triad of training (sikkhattaya)—the group of virtue, the group of concentration, and the group of wisdom—are called 'Vinaya' because they are like discipline. The three trainings, which constitute the giving of the Teacher's instruction, are referred to as "anusiṭṭhidānavasena" (by way of giving instruction).

"Sammādiṭṭhipaccayattā" means because it is the cause for Right View. This is because Right View becomes fulfilled for one who practices the three trainings. In accordance with the statement, "Therefore, monk, you should first purify the very beginning of wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? Well-purified virtue and straight view (diṭṭhi)," the three trainings are preceded by Right View. In these two senses, the three trainings are called "diṭṭhi" by way of metonymy, attributing the name of the effect to the cause (phalūpacāra) and the name of the cause to the effect (kāraṇူpacāra). Alternatively, it is intended to refer to them by way of the wholesome states that are their own parts. The three trainings are called Vinaya because they are the Buddha's act of disciplining. That disciplining occurs through the Dhamma, which is of an even (righteous) nature, or through the Dhamma of the teaching, and not through punishment with a stick etc.; thus it is called "Dhamma-vinaya."

It is for the sake of Nibbāna, which is the supreme faultless state, or for the sake of the unshakable liberation of mind (the fruit of Arahantship). The three trainings, which are the cause for knowing through higher knowledge (abhijñā) etc. regarding the states to be fully known (abhiññeyya) etc., are called "Dhamma-vinaya." The phrase "in this [dispensation]" is repeated to make a definition (limitation) from other dispensations. Alternatively, with the intention that the word "eva" (only) has been elided, it is said, "niyamော kato" (a definition has been made).

In the word "bhikkhuko," the syllable "ka" is added without changing the meaning, thus the meaning is given as "having the nature of begging" (bhikkhana-dhammatā). In the reading "bhikkhako," the meaning is "one who begs." Dirt mixed with dust is called "jallika," while pure dirt without dust is called "mala." Because the word 'bhikkhu' is well-established for a person who wears torn cloth, the definition is given as "bhinnapaṭadhara" (one who wears torn robes).

One for whom there remains a limit (odhi) of the path to be developed and defilements to be abandoned is called "odhiso." An Arahant, however, is without limit (odhirahita) because of the absence of such remainder. Therefore, it is said, "A bhikkhu is anodhiso due to the abandoning of defilements." Alternatively, the word "odhi" is well-established in the sense of a part. Since all paths have been developed and all defilements have been abandoned by an Arahant, they are not called "odhi." It should be understood that this definition "pahānā" (abandoning) is stated by way of the synonym for destroying (bhedana) [the defilements].
178:
By the word beginning with "sekha," the meaning expressed by the word *bhikkhu* is shown by way of virtue (*guṇa*). Below, however, it is shown by way of designation (*samaññā*) and profession (*paṭiññā*), and by way of etymological definition (*nibbacana*) with the word beginning with "bhikkhati."

By the words "sekho bhikkhu," the seven types of trainees (*sekha*) are spoken of. By the words "bhinnattā pāpakānaṃ...pe... bhikkhu," only the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is spoken of. These two do not agree with the [other] two: "by the word *sekha*, the seven noble ones along with the virtuous worldling (*kalyāṇa-puthujjana*); and by the word *bhinnattā*, the four established in the fruit (*phalaṭṭha*)." It should be understood that this disagreement is a direct (*nippariyāya*) presentation, not a figurative one. It was said, "In other places, the virtuous worldling and so forth are spoken of." Is it not also spoken of one who is a *bhikkhu* by profession (*paṭiññā*)? It is spoken of; however, here, because only a *bhikkhu* capable of producing all types of jhāna is intended, that [other] person is not intended.

The word of the Blessed One is called "ṭhāna" (ground/basis) because it is the cause for performing the act of higher ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*). That which is suitable for that word is called "ṭhānāraha." It means a formal act (*kammavācā*) with an undiminished motion (*ñatti*) and which is not recited out of order.

It means that it is virtue (*sīla*) in the primary sense because it is abstinence by undertaking (*samādāna-virati*) and abstinence by non-transgression (*avītikkamana-virati*). Referring to non-covetousness (*anabhijjhā*) and so forth, the figurative nature of mental virtue (*cetasika-sīla*) is mentioned. They say a city-builder is a master of the science of building sites (*vatthuvijjā-cariya*). The four types of nutriment are *asita* (eaten food) and so forth; or they are food to be chewed, eaten, licked, or sucked.

One endowed with the restraint of the Pātimokkha has closed faculties, because the three types of good conduct have the restraint of the faculties as their nutriment. Or, the restraint of the Pātimokkha is a strong dependence (*upanissaya*) for the restraint of the faculties. Thus, one whose faculties are closed by the restraint of the Pātimokkha is called "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha" (*pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuta*). With this intention, the meaning of the word "saṃvuta" is given as "one with closed faculties." It should be understood that the phrase "by the Pātimokkha and by restraint" is said with the intention that virtue other than the Pātimokkha is included by the mention of bodily non-transgression and so forth. The second meaning is stated referring to the identical meaning of both terms.

Intending that even covetousness and so forth are included by the phrase "all immorality" (*sabbampi dussīlyaṃ*), it is said, "he practices even with the mind; therefore, to show that." "Therein" refers to the improper conducts (*anācāra*) spoken of by way of bodily transgression and so forth. "He incurs the disposal of heavy articles" means he incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave) offense.
179:
"Āropima" refers to bamboo that has grown spontaneously on the Saṅgha's land. "Phātikamma" is the act of making something other than a heavy article (*garubhaṇḍa*) become a heavy article. By the Pali term "daṇḍakamma," the previously mentioned manual labor is meant. Because they bathe with powders such as siris-bark powder, that substance is called "sināna" (bath powder, etc., which is the cause of bathing).

One who habitually speaks pleasant words, whether true or false, is called "cāṭu" (a flatterer). The desire to be a speaker of pleasant words is called "cāṭukāma," and that state is called "cāṭukamyatā" (flattery). It means there is no place where mung bean soup cannot enter, as it is not incompatible with any food. This is the opinion of the commentator. He is called "paribhaṭa" because he carries/supports or because he nourishes. Or, a servant (*sevaka*) who is an attendant is called "paribhaṭa."

"Bhaṇḍāgārikakamma" refers to the work of a storekeeper performed for laypeople. Giving food first in order to receive food is called "piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍa." Or, accepting food offered in return after giving one's own food is called "piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍa." Managing the requisites of the Saṅgha and the requisites of the Cetiya in an improper way, or misusing items meant for the Saṅgha and Cetiya, or treating them as one's own property, as some teachers say.

It is called "gocara" (pasture/resort) because cattle graze in this place. It is called "gocara" because it is like a grazing ground for cattle. It is a place that should be frequented constantly. Or, "cattle" refers to the faculties such as the eye. The objects such as forms, which are the range of those faculties, are called "gocara." Since an unsuitable resort is called "agocara," a suitable resort other than that is called "gocara."

Because the word "vā" also has the meaning of shaking off (removing), he said "viniddhutakibbisāni vā."

They are called "oramattaka" (trifling/minor) because they have a limit that is the least of these faults. Faults that should be remedied or removed merely by restraint of body and speech are called "saṃyamakaraṇīya." Acts to be performed merely by mental restraint, such as "I will not do this again," or by the restraint of the faculties, are called "saṃvarakaraṇīya." One who habitually lives in the Divivihāra district is called "divivihāravāsī." The mental determination itself is called "adhiṭṭhānāvikamma." Here, the confession (*desanā*) is intended by "vuṭṭhānāvikamma." Therein, according to the teaching "to be performed by the arising of thought, connected with attention," it refers to faults that should not be transgressed and do not lead to an offense, for the sake of purifying the restraint of the Pātimokkha; this is the teacher's intention.

"Catubbidhassa" refers to the four fears: the fear of self-reproach, the fear of reproach by others, the fear of punishment, and the fear of an unhappy destination.

Intending that only a monk is meant by the text "idha bhikkhu," he said, "As for the remaining trainings, they are mentioned to show the meaning of the word *sikkhā* by way of extracting the meaning."
180:
The inclusion of the term 'bhikkhu' is done for the purpose of showing all four assemblies capable of producing all jhānas, by placing the foremost assembly at the head. Alternatively, because a monk is intended by way of virtue, it should be understood that all training (sikkhā) is intended here.

In the phrase 'sabbena sikkhāsamaādānena' (by the undertaking of all training), it refers to that undertaking by which all training rules are undertaken. Even if it is a single undertaking, it is called 'sabbasamādāna' (undertaking of all) because it performs the function of undertaking all training. In the case of multiple undertakings, there is no need to even mention it. 'Sabbena sikkhitabbākārena' (by every mode of training) refers to modes such as non-transgression, confession of offenses, rehabilitation from offenses, and the practice of duties. With reference to making the remaining training rules complete without exception through the power of non-transgression, the words 'bhinnassapi' and so forth are spoken.

Considering that meditation which purifies the mind from the obstructing hindrances (nīvaraṇa) is the devotion to wakefulness (jāgariyānuyoga), the word 'bhāvanaṃ' (meditation) is spoken. 'Suppapariggāhakaṃ' refers to the clear comprehension (sampajañña) that distinguishes and grasps, thinking: 'This sleep does not exist before or after this (cognitive process); this (fatigue) is the cause of this sleep,' and so forth.

520-521. 'Yutto' means exerting effort. It shows the connection that one is devoted to wakefulness while maintaining continuous effort (sātacca) and mature wisdom (nepakka).

Regarding the phrase 'lokiyāyapi... āha', it means that in the development of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā), states such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) do not occur together on a single object. Even when they do occur, the faculties (indriya) and powers (bala) that arise are included only within the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga). This is because it is said, 'Joy (pāmojja) has faith as its strong supporting cause' (S.ii.23); thus, by taking the enlightenment factor of rapture (pīti-sambojjhaṅga), the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) and the power of faith (saddhā-bala), which are its strong supporting causes, are also taken. It should be understood that this is said with reference to the fact that only five path factors occur at the moment of insight.

Knowing the purposeful (sātthaka) and so forth in every mode, or rightly, or evenly, is 'sampajāna'; that itself is 'sampajañña' (clear comprehension). By that (sampajañña), because of its association with mindfulness, although mindfulness is not mentioned in the brief exposition (uddesa), it is intended to be spoken of by the word 'sato' in the detailed exposition (niddesa).

Knowing the purposeful nature of advancing and so forth is 'sātthaka-sampajañña' (clear comprehension of purpose). Likewise, there is 'sappāya-sampajañña' (clear comprehension of suitability). In the matters of advancing and so forth, whether at the place of alms-round or elsewhere, knowing without abandoning the resort (gocara) known as the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is 'gocara-sampajañña' (clear comprehension of the resort). Non-delusion in advancing and so forth is itself 'asammoha-sampajañña' (clear comprehension of non-delusion).
181:
The 'two kinds of speech' refer to speech regarding following instructions and not following instructions, which were not mentioned before. It means one only follows the instructions; because of being easy to admonish (suvaca), one gives a reply (speaks back).

'By the head of the meditation subject' (kammaṭṭhāna-sīsena) means by the excellence of the meditation subject, making the meditation subject the priority. By that phrase, it shows the meaning of going to the shrine without abandoning the meditation subject that will be mentioned in the passage 'the bowl is also insentient' and so forth, or the meditation subject that is currently being maintained. The word 'tasmā' (therefore) connects with the sentence 'dhammakathā kathetabbāyevāti vadanti' (they say that a Dhamma talk should indeed be given). 'Bhaye' refers to times of danger, such as the power of other kings.

'Avasesaṭṭhāne' refers to the place after the gruel has been taken. The mention of standing and walking is said by way of the postures that should be determined, not by way of rejecting sitting which must definitely be done at times such as eating.

The Elder Dārucīriya—
'Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: In the seen, there will be only the seen; in the heard, the sensed, and the cognized, there will be only the heard, the sensed, and the cognized. When, Bāhiya, for you, in the seen there is only the seen, and in the heard, the sensed, and the cognized there is only the heard, the sensed, and the cognized, then, Bāhiya, you will not be "with that." When, Bāhiya, you are not "with that," then, Bāhiya, you will not be "in that." When, Bāhiya, you are not "in that," then, Bāhiya, you will be neither here nor beyond nor in between the two. This itself is the end of suffering.' (Ud. 10)—
With just this much Dhamma, he realized the fruit of Arahantship.

Moving to the side to avoid a stump and so forth, or to avoid the foot that is planted, is called 'vītiharaṇa'. Alternatively, bringing the back foot up to the planted foot is 'atiharaṇa', and bringing it beyond that is 'vītiharaṇa'. This is the distinction between atiharaṇa and vītiharaṇa. 'Avīci' means without interval.

Regarding the phrase 'even in the first impulsion (javana)... does not occur', this is said with reference to the absence of lust and so forth for 'woman' or 'man' in the five-sense-door cognitive process (pañcavijñāṇavīthi). For in that process, through the power of unwise adverting and determining (ayoniso āvajjana-votthabbana), lust arises for a pleasant female form and so forth, and aversion arises for an unpleasant one. However, in the mind-door (manodvāra), lust and so forth for 'woman' or 'man' do occur.
182: The root of that mind-door impulsion (manodvārajavana) is the five-door impulsion (pañcadvārajavana), or all the consciousness starting from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) as previously mentioned. Thus, the primary knowledge (mūlapariññā) is stated by fully understanding the life-continuum, which is the root of mind-door impulsion. Adventitiousness (āgantukatā) and temporariness (tāvakālikatā), however, occur by virtue of the five-door impulsion not having occurred before and lasting only for a moment. It is said that the Maṇisappa (gem-snake) is a species of snake found on the island of Ceylon (Sīhaḷadīpa). Calana means vibration. Atiharati means bringing up to the mouth. Vītiharati means bringing from the mouth to the stomach, or bringing food that has reached the stomach to the side. Allattañca anupāleti means protecting it so that it does not become excessively dry due to wind and so forth. Ābujati means reflecting on or knowing the searching for food, swallowing, digestion, and indigestion, etc. The effort (payoga) that accomplishes this knowing is called 'right effort' (sammāpayoga). Alternatively, knowing that 'relying on the right practice, there is no such person as a 'self' (attā) who is the consumer within' is called ābujana (reflection). Aṭṭhāne refers to unsuitable places occupied by humans or non-humans, such as fields, shrines, and so forth. Tumbato means from a water vessel such as a bamboo tube. Taṃ refers to discarded water. Gate means in the act of going. Since the bringing of the body forward and backward in going was already mentioned by the inclusion of abhikkama (advancing) and paṭikkama (receding), it should be understood that here only the act of going itself is taken. Or, the following meaning is the distinction between these words. Ettakena means that the clear comprehension of the resort (gocarasampajañña) is not yet evident merely by mentioning the maintenance of the four postures without abandoning the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Thus, just as the meditation subject is not evident during sleep, for one who discerns the phenomena occurring in walking, standing, and sitting, the phenomena occurring during sleep are not evident. Impulsion (javana) is called 'functional process' (kiriyāmayapavatta) because it causes bodily and other actions, and because it arises due to functional advertence (āvajjana-kiriyā). Or, all thought-processes (vīthicitta) occurring in the six doors are called functional processes. The second jhāna is called 'tuṇhībhāva' (silence) because it is devoid of verbal formations (vacīsaṅkhāra), namely vitakka and vicāra. Upāsanatthāna means the place for practicing and exerting in the meditation subject, like the place where archers practice their archery. To show that very meaning, it is called 'yogapatha' (the path of practice). Sīsaṃ dhovati (washing the head) signifies reaching the state of a free man after being liberated from the slavery of evil desires. Or, it is the washing away of the dust of ill-repute cast by those who practice wrongly.
183: According to the Vinaya method, it appears in the Pārājika on taking what is not given (adinnādāna). According to the Suttanta method, it appears in the Āraññaka training rule referring to a forest-dwelling monk, as 'pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchimaṃ' (at most five hundred bow-lengths). This is because that monk is described in the Suttas as 'āraññako pantasenāsano' (a forest-dweller in a remote lodging) due to living in the forest according to the Vinaya method. The place called 'nitumba' or 'nadīkuñja' is known as 'kandara' (a grotto or cleft). It is shown that even in non-mountainous regions, a place where river water recedes and is difficult to traverse is called a 'kandara'. By the phrase 'bhājetvā dassitaṃ' (shown by classification), the reason for the necessity of detailed classification and for providing the detailed explanation at the end is shown. An action performed in a secluded place is called 'rahassa'; that which is suitable or fit for that action is called 'rāhasseyyaka'. This is because Taddhita suffixes are diverse. Alternatively, a good action in seclusion is called 'rahassa', and that which is fit for it is 'rāhasseyyaka'. Paṇihita means well-placed (well-established). Pariggahitaniyyānaṃ means having the nature of deliverance through the grasping of the body and so forth. It means being endowed with the nature of deliverance due to the proper occurrence in objects such as the body. Alternatively, the knowledge that grasps the body and so forth is called 'pariggaha'; because of being associated with that knowledge, it means having established mindfulness which is grasped and is a means of deliverance. 542-543. 'Vikārappattiyā' means by way of the state of the mind reaching alteration. 'Sabbasaṅgāhikavasena' means by way of including all anger occurring towards beings and formations. It should be understood that the inclusion of all is done because the abandonment by eradication (samucchedappahāna) is intended. 'Idaṃ sandhāya' (referring to this) refers to the words 'dve dhammā' (two qualities). Although 'thinamiddha' (sloth and torpor) is indicated in the singular, in the detailed explanation (niddesa), the plural 'santā' is used, thus making a difference in number. The phrase 'nirodhasantatāya' (by the peacefulness of cessation) is used to exclude the peacefulness of the factors (aṅgasantatāya) or the peacefulness of nature (sabhāvasantatāya). The perception that is the opposite of sloth and torpor, being free from the alteration of sloth and torpor, is called 'ālokasaññā' (perception of light). Therefore, it is said, 'This perception is luminous'. Terms such as 'vantattā muttattā' and 'ālokā hoti' are called 'cattattā', etc. Or, by the word 'ādi' (and so forth), both...
184:
Collecting the terms of the description (niddesa), among those terms, whichever are synonyms (vevacana) of each other, it should be understood that it is said "they are synonyms of each other" with reference to those terms. By the word "paṭimuñcato", he shows the overcoming (abhibhava) accompanied by exertion (sārambha). Because of attending (ābhujati) and knowing (sampajānāti) without hindrance (nirāvaraṇa), it is called "nirāvaraṇābhoga". Because it has the nature of attending without hindrance, it is called "open" (vivaṭa).

It should be understood that remorse (vippaṭisāra) based on the transgression of an object (vatthujjhācāra) due to indecision such as "Is it past noon or not?" is called by the term "transgression of an object" (vatthujjhācāra) as a causal designation.

Regarding the word "kilissanti", they say it means "they defile" (kilesenti). Or, they themselves are defiled by the nature of distress (sadaratha). This is because when those hindrances (nīvaraṇa) arise, they do not arise free from defilement.

In this very Vibhaṅga, the word "upeto hoti" and so on have already been taught in the sections on the restraint of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkhasaṃvara) and so forth.

"By way of description" (niddesavasena) means they say it is by way of description (niddesa) such as "Among those, what is equanimity? That which is equanimity..." and by way of re-description (paṭiniddesa) such as "He is endowed with this equanimity." By this description, "Among those, what is... he is endowed with this equanimity," the person (puggala) is indicated. By the re-description "samupeto" and so on, he is indicated again. Or, the person is indicated up to the word "samannāgato". By this re-description, "Therefore he is called upekkhako," the person is indicated again. In this way, the description and re-description should be connected by way of those words. "By way of variety" (pakārena) means they establish the meaning of the word "upekkhako" by way of the variety of the Dhamma such as "upekkhana" (the act of looking on) and by way of the variety of the person such as "upeto samupeto". The meaning "upekkhana" is the cause for the meaning "upekkhā". This is because the meaning "upekkhā" exists by way of looking on (upekkhana). Similarly, the meaning "upāgato samupāgato" is the cause for the meanings "upeto samupeto". In this way, desiring to show the cause of each meaning by way of the Dhamma and the person, they explain it. Or, they explain it by showing the cause for the meaning of "upekkhako" itself by way of "He is endowed with this equanimity" and so on. They analyze by showing the variety of syllables (byañjana) such as "upekkhana, ajjhupekkhana, samupeto". Or, the separate explanation of the meaning of "upekkhā" included within the word "upekkhako" and the word "upekkhako" itself is given as "That which is equanimity is called upekkhana" and so on, and "He is endowed with this equanimity" and so on...
185:
This is the analysis of syllables (byañjanavibhāga). The state of being overturned so as not to be known in every way is called "aññātatā" (unknownness). Even if known in some way, the state of not being able to be delimited without remainder is called "gambhīrabhāva" (profundity).

This phrase "uparibhūmippattiyā" should be applied only to this place: "rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā" (surpassing perceptions of form). Or, since the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) etc. are also higher planes (uparibhūmi) than the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāsānañcāyatana) etc., it is not illogical in all places; it is indeed appropriate.

In the description of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana-niddesa), in the Pali passage "anantaṃ viññāṇaṃ" and so on, "tena vuccati anantaṃ viññāṇaṃ", the word "viññāṇena" is an instrumental case (karaṇavacana) used in the sense of the accusative case. It is said in the Commentary that one attends to the consciousness that pervades that very space-concept. Or, the meaning of this Pali is: one attends to the consciousness pervading that space-concept with the Viññāṇañcāyatana-consciousness. However, only this meaning is appropriate: having pervaded that space-concept with consciousness, one attends to it according to the mode grasped by that consciousness; thus, that consciousness pervades infinitely. "Because it is not mentioned" means that after speaking generally as "knowledge in those resultants (vipāka)," it is not mentioned specifically. In this Abhidhamma classification method, because functional (kiriya) states do not have the nature of producing results, their status as "dhamma" (cause) is not mentioned.

If that is so, since functional states do not have resultant fruits, should their status as "attha" (result) also not be mentioned? No, [it should be mentioned] because they are conditioned states (paccayuppanna) produced by causes. If their status as "attha" is asserted because they are conditioned, then since wholesome (kusala) and unwholesome (akusala) states can also be conditioned, do they not also become "attha"? This is not prohibited. However, because they are prominent as the primary causes of results, only their status as "dhamma" is mentioned.

If it is asked, "Since functional states are conditions, do they not also become 'dhamma'?" This is not a fault, as it is not prohibited [that they are causes]. However, because functional states are not the cause of the state connected with the fruit of kamma, their status as "dhamma" is not mentioned.

Alternatively, for one who reflects on wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional states only by their nature (sabhāva), without making a distinction such as "this is the cause of this, this is the result produced by the cause," both Dhamma-paṭisambhidā and Attha-paṭisambhidā occur. For this reason also, it should be understood that their status as attha and dhamma is not mentioned [in the usual sequence].

In the sections on wholesome and unwholesome states, Dhamma-paṭisambhidā is able to see the causal status, the specific potency, and the result to be produced; thus, it looks toward the result to be produced. Therefore, in connection with that result to be produced, it is said, "Knowledge in those resultants is Attha-paṭisambhidā." The function of Attha-paṭisambhidā is merely seeing the nature, because it sees only the finished result. Since that Attha-paṭisambhidā does not look toward the producing cause, it should be understood that in the section on resultants, it is not said, "Knowledge in those ripening states is Dhamma-paṭisambhidā."

In the Abhidhamma Classification as well, since the teaching by way of the arising of consciousness is an exhaustive teaching, the statement "By which knowledge one knows those knowledges," spoken by way of the objects already shown, does not prohibit having other objects. Relying on the stronger Pali text, the intended meaning of the other Pali text should be sought. The supreme state is Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). The Buddhas are called 'Āsabhā' (Supreme) either because they proceed towards Omniscient Knowledge by virtue of their declaration, or because they are approached by the eight assemblies. By the phrase 'Idaṃ pana,' it refers to Omniscient Knowledge itself as the station of the Buddhas. 'Tiṭṭhamāno vā' means that even if not speaking, merely by standing, it is considered a declaration. Regarding the eight assemblies, the Buddha roars a courageous roar, being endowed with the unshakable knowledge shown by the words: "Sāriputta, I know many hundreds of assemblies of Khattiyas... I do not see any reason why fear or hesitation would overcome me in those assemblies." (This is to be understood) through the Sīhanāda Sutta found in the Khandhaka Vaggas.

By the remainder of the sutta, "The four wheels (Catu-cakka) of devas and humans turn," it should be understood that the term 'cakka' (wheel) in that sutta refers to the sequential occurrence of the wheels of success, which are the results of causes such as relying on good people (sappurisu-passaya), or the continuous occurrence of subsequent wheels of success based on previous ones. Because the task of penetration is completed, the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship is called 'Paṭivedha' (Penetration), and it is said to "arise at the moment of the Fruit (Phala)." The completion of the function of the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa), which has the benefit of pointing out to others what has been attained through that penetration, occurs merely by the realization; thus it is said to "occur at the moment of the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) of Aññāsi Koṇḍañña." Thereafter, the occurrence of the knowledge of teaching until Parinibbāna should be understood as the station of that Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka) which has been set in motion, just like the station of the wheel-treasure of a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) whose wheel has been set in motion.

They are called 'Samādānāni' because they are well-undertaken; regarding those undertakings, it is said "those performed after having undertaken them." Alternatively, by saying that kamma itself is 'Kamma-samādāna,' it shows that there is no new meaning in the word 'samādāna,' just as in the word 'muttagata,' the word 'gata' (has no separate meaning).

'Agatigāminī' refers to the practice leading to Nibbāna. For was it not taught: "Sāriputta, I know Nibbāna, and I know the practice leading to Nibbāna"?

'Hānabhāgiya-dhamma' refers to states that have the nature of decline, or states such as perceptions associated with sense-desire (kāma-sahagata-saññā). 'Taṃ kāraṇaṃ' refers to previously performed volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra), and so forth.

This word 'Idāni' should be read in conjunction with the phrase "should be understood as having been taught in this sequence." By dividing the terms 'obstruction of defilements' (kilesāvaraṇa) and 'the absence of that,' it refers to the absence of the obstruction of defilements. For the attainment of the destruction of defilements, the obstruction of defilements is not the cause (aṭṭhāna), but only the absence of that obstruction is the cause (ṭhāna). For non-attainment, the obstruction of defilements is the cause, while the absence of that obstruction is not the cause.
199:
The absence of that (obstruction) is not the cause (aṭṭhāna). In that context, by taking the absence of that obstruction, the Buddha sees the existence of Right View (Sammādiṭṭhi) such as "there is that which is given," etc., and the absence of the cause for Wrong View (Micchādiṭṭhi) which is the opposite of that Right View. To establish this meaning—that the Blessed One, with this knowledge, sees the obstruction of defilements and its absence, which are the causes and non-causes for attainment and non-attainment—it is said: "Because of seeing the existence of mundane Right View and because of seeing the absence of the cause for fixed Wrong View (Niyata-micchādiṭṭhi)." Here, only the seeing of the cause for attainment is intended, because later, the seeing of the absence of the obstruction of result (vipākāvaraṇa) by power of the capable person (bhabba-puggala) will be discussed. However, it should be understood that other attainments and non-attainments are also mentioned here by implication, as they are accomplished by this knowledge. 'Because of seeing the diversity of elements' (Dhātu-vematta) means seeing the diversity of elements associated with lust (rāga), etc., by power of their intensity; or seeing the causes of temperament (cariya) such as "this person is of lustful temperament because this element is intense"; or it means seeing the diversity of elements like lust, etc., as lust and so forth are themselves elements by their intrinsic nature. 'Without taking effort' (Payogaṃ anādiyitvā) means preaching by power of liberation without regarding the effort associated with sensual lust or ill-will, as in the cases of the Minister Santati, Aṅgulimāla, and others.

## 1. Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā

In the phrase 'Na hetum eva,' the meaning is 'Na hetū eva' (they are not causes). For the sake of euphony (vyañjana-siliṭṭhatā), the vowel is shortened and the letter 'ma' is inserted, as in the word 'adukkhamasukhā.' In the phrase 'By this method also,' the distinction should be understood that the former method negates the state of being a cause, while the latter method includes the category of states that are not causes (na-hetu-dhamma).

By the word 'Cuti' (death), one should understand the taking of a single birth bounded by death. By the word 'Bhava' (existence), the existence taught in nine ways is taken. By the state of being included within those (destinies and existences), they are said to be 'included' in those respective places. By the phrase 'Only that which is cognizable by mind-consciousness as it arises,' the distinction of these (fivefold consciousnesses) from matter (rūpa) is made, as "matter is not like that which is cognizable by the six consciousnesses as it arises."

'Even passing from aeon to aeon, it does not arise' means it never arises in that manner (with different doors or objects). It shows that these fivefold consciousnesses do not have a diversity of characteristics different from what has been stated, unlike milk and other substances (which change into curd, etc.).

'Having combined' means having combined all matter existing in the world. By this, while showing the non-manifestation even in greatness, he cuts off the quibble that it would not be manifest due to subtlety.
200:
The pedantic argument that "it will not be made manifest" is cut off. "In my physical basis, which is the eye-sensitivity" is the meaning. "Visaya" is intended as the locus of sovereignty (domain).

"Abbokiṇṇā" means unobstructed, having no interval. It means that by this word "anantarā," the fixed sequence (paṭipāṭiniyama) of the five consciousnesses, which are distinct, is negated. "Anantaratā" means that the state of the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) is negated by this Pali. By the word "samanantaratā," the state of the contiguity condition (samanantara-paccaya) is also negated.

"Ābhujanato" means because of performing a turn, like a rotation, or because of causing to turn back. Here also, "the five consciousnesses are without advertence (anābhoga)" means they do not have the nature of advertence (ābhoga-sabhāva), which is like turning. In the Pali passages such as "the five consciousnesses have no adverting (āvaṭṭana)," the meaning should be understood as the absence of the function of adverting (āvaṭṭanabhāva).

In this Pali, "does not specifically cognize any phenomenon (dhamma)," the word "dhamma" does not include all phenomena such as visible forms; rather, it is said, "Mind is the forerunner of all states (dhammā)," in order to show the intended phenomenon.

The impact upon visible forms and so on means the meeting of those consciousnesses with the visible forms; since this is appropriate to say, it is stated as "the mere impact (abhinipāta) of visible forms and so on." Alternatively, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative (kamma). This is because visible forms and so on are what should be impacted by the consciousnesses. The intended meaning in the passages beginning with "This is what is meant" is as follows: excluding visible forms and so on which should be known by making them objects, these five consciousnesses do not have the cognition of wholesome and unwholesome volition, the states associated with that volition, and the states such as adverting which are the forerunners of the aforementioned five consciousnesses and which should be known by them. By doing so, he prohibits functions other than seeing and so on, stating, "These five consciousnesses do not have what is called specific cognition (paṭiviññatti) of wholesome states and so on, which is distinct from the mere function of seeing (dassana) and so on."

Because of the state of being non-resultant (avipāka), he includes wholesome and unwholesome states without excluding other general indeterminate (abyākata) states. He also prohibits the function ending with death (cuti). By the word "pi," process-consciousnesses (vīthicitta) together with javana are combined, and the intention in prohibiting them at the five doors would be: "If with a corrupted mind... with a confident mind, one speaks or acts"—only those powerful states occurring at the sixth door (mind-door) which perform speaking and acting as preached, and those similar states which produce happiness and suffering, are taken by the word "dhamma." Therefore, there is no cognition of those states by the javana occurring at the five doors. However, cognition by way of being a forerunner of the weak five-door processes is not prohibited therein.
201:
"Does not initiate bodily action, nor initiate vocal action" is understood because of the permission of weak mental action, by negating the initiation of only the production of consciousness that causes the two types of intimation (viññatti). Likewise, the undertaking of wholesome or unwholesome states, such as "I will perform wholesome bodily conduct," or its opposite, "I will perform unwholesome action," does not occur by means of javana at the five doors. Similarly, in the explanation of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), it is said: "Death (cuti) at the five doors also does not occur by five-door consciousnesses, because the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) does not occur in those doors." This is the meaning.

There is the Pali: "By the five consciousnesses, one does not cognize any phenomenon (dhamma) other than the mere impact (abhinipāta)." In that Pali, the meaning is clear: excluding the mere impact of visible forms and so on, one cannot cognize any other nature of phenomena. This is because even though eye-consciousness receives a visible form, it cannot grasp it as "a visible form." Since the receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchana) also does not have the cognition of aspects such as the blue color of the visible form, the cognition of any phenomenon is negated. However, because there is an excellent cognition of that object by the five consciousnesses, it is not said (of sampaṭicchana, etc.) that it is "other than the mere impact." For those who desire the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā) other than that for which the Pali states the nature of having external and present objects, the co-arising of the analytical knowledge with five-door javana is prohibited. "Rūpārūpadhamme" means the states of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara).

Why is it said, "One does not wake up by five-door consciousness"? Is it not that when visible forms and so on come into the focus (āpātha), one wakes up from sleep? No, it is not so. To show that the mind-door javana arises first, he said "niddāyantassa hi," etc. Some teachers say it is only indeterminate (abyākata) because, being enticed by a true dream, mere adverting arises. It should be understood that those teachers intend that even in the mind-door, adverting arises two or three times, stands in the place of javana, and then subsides into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

"Tassā eva vasena" means that by the power of that wisdom alone, it is the locus of knowledge in another way; the words should be construed as "it should be known."

## 3. The Explanation of the Exposition of the Triads

'Paññā-pariṇāmitesu' means [in spheres of work, etc.] that have been ripened (brought to completion) by wisdom. The term 'yoga-vihitesu' (arranged by application) is merely a specification of the object where wisdom is established. Therefore, all past, present, and future spheres of work, etc., that are arranged by wisdom should be understood as 'yoga-vihita'. An art that must be learned and then performed is called 'sippa' (craft), while other work [performed without learning] is called 'kamma' (action). This is the distinction between the two. In the term 'vaḍḍhakī-kamma' (carpentry), the coarse work that can be done without learning should be understood as 'kamma'. Alternatively, wisdom itself in those various instances should be known as 'kamma' or 'sippa'. What is called 'nāga-maṇḍala' is the art of removing poison by forming a circle, summoning snakes with mantras, and giving offerings. 'Paritta' (protection) is the art of guarding against danger, and by that art, people remove poison by blowing with the mouth, saying 'phū'. The mantra for curing [bites from] spiders and such is called 'phu-dhamanaka-mantra'. The brief matrices starting with 'A, Ā' and the various detailed forms starting with 'Ka, Kā' are called 'lekhā' (the art of writing).

Wholesome states are 'one's own property' (because they bring welfare and happiness). Other unwholesome states are 'not one's own property' (because they bring harm and suffering). The four truths that are to be penetrated should be understood as 'anulomana' (conformity) by way of being the cause for such penetration. Previously, wisdom was spoken of by terms such as 'yoga-vihitesu vā kamma-yatanesu', and again, it was spoken of as 'anulomika-khanti' (conformity-patience), etc., by way of synonyms for that wisdom; with this intention, it was said, 'anulomika... etc., are synonyms for wisdom'. Here, 'evarūpiṃ' (of such a nature) means having the objects such as the aforementioned spheres of work, having the nature of conformity to the truth of ownership of deeds (kammassakatā), and having the mode of occurrence such as impermanence. The aforementioned descriptions of the planes, natures, and modes of occurrence should be connected with patience (khanti), etc. That wisdom which can endure the reflection—defined as the function of absolute scrutiny and specific knowing of states (such as spheres of work)—because it has an undistorted nature, is called 'dhamma-nijjhānakkhanti' (patience in reflecting on the Dhamma), meaning that in that wisdom, there is the capacity to endure the reflection on states.

Because it abandons non-restraint (asaṃvara), the volition associated with the abstinence of undertaking (samādāna-virati) and the abstinence of encountering (sampatta-virati) is called 'the volition of release (muñca-cetanā) of one fulfilling virtue'. Since the nature of being consisting in giving and virtue of the wisdom occurring in the preceding and succeeding moments has been stated, it is appropriate to say 'ārabbha' (beginning) by way of the volition of release and the subsequent volition, and 'adhikicca' (concerning) by way of the preceding volition; thus, the reading 'adhikiccā' is also suitable.
203:
The five precepts and the ten precepts are included in the formations and existences (saṅkhāra-bhava) which are the causes of consciousness and birth; they have been included in the Dhamma-ṭṭhiti text beginning with 'Uppādā vā' (Whether [Tathāgatas] arise). The prescription of virtue that brings about [favorable] existence, even if it is heard [from the Buddha], is not dependent solely on the Buddha's teaching (as it can also occur outside the dispensation); thus, this prescription of virtue was spoken of for bhikkhus and others.

Wisdom included within higher wisdom (adhipaññā) is called 'wisdom belonging to higher wisdom'. Alternatively, the term 'adhipaññā' should be understood as referring to the states (Path and Fruit) produced by higher wisdom, or the states (insight) that are the basis for that higher wisdom; the wisdom occurring in those states is called 'wisdom belonging to higher wisdom'.

Thinking whether skill in bringing about ruin could be 'apāya-kosalla' (skill in loss), one asks: 'How can skill in loss be called wisdom?' To refute that person's intention, [the Buddha] said: 'Only one who has wisdom...', etc. 'Tatrūpāyā' means the means (wisdom) in those various matters. The arising [of that knowledge] at the occasion of its occurrence is called 'ṭhānuppatti' (presence of mind). What is that knowledge? It is the knowing of the cause; it means arising quickly at that very place (at that very moment) when danger, etc., arise.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Triads is finished.

## 4. The Explanation of the Exposition of the Tetrads

'He does not yearn or tremble' (na paritassati) means he does not yearn, thinking 'It would be good if I had provisions such as rice,' or he does not tremble because of the absence of those provisions.

'Not dependent on others' (aparappaccaya) means not being made to believe by others. 'Knowledge of the Dhamma' (dhamme ñāṇaṃ) means knowledge having the four truths as its object. Indeed, the noble truths are called 'Dhamma' because they have an undistorted nature. Alternatively, the Noble Path, which is the best among conditioned things, and its fruit are called 'Dhamma'; the wisdom associated with that Path and Fruit is 'knowledge of the Dhamma'. It is not the producing of another knowledge or the leading of a method, but rather it is the function of reviewing knowledge; with this intention, it is said: 'the function of reviewing knowledge'. Here, 'by this Dhamma' (iminā dhammena) means by the knowledge of the Path; however, since both the knowledge of the Path and the Fruit are the basis for reviewing and the cause for leading the method, it is not inappropriate to say 'by those two dhammas'. Likewise, because the Dhamma of the four truths has been known, and because the Dhamma called Path and Fruit has reached association with right view that penetrates the truths, it is the leading of the method; therefore, this...
204:
The meaning "by the Dhamma known either as an object of knowledge or by association with knowledge" is also not inappropriate (it is indeed appropriate). Although they know suffering in all its aspects—past, future, and present—because there is a particular firm application of mind to the present suffering included within one's own continuity, it is said: "not only that (past and future), but also this (present)." It is called Nayana-ñāṇa (or Naya-ñāṇa) because of the inference regarding the unseen Truth through the seen Truth. It is called Kāraṇa-ñāṇa because it is the cause for seeing the unseen Truth. Alternatively, since the word kāraṇa expresses a suitable meaning, it means knowledge conformable to the knowledge of the Dhamma (Anurūpa-ñāṇa).

Conventional knowledge (Sammuti-ñāṇa) refers to knowledge included among those things designated as knowledge by the mere generality of knowing that illuminates the object, without the extraordinary function of penetration like the knowledge of the Dhamma and others. Alternatively, it is called Sammuti-ñāṇa because it occurs by way of convention. The remaining knowledge, being dissimilar to the other three types of knowledge, is to be understood as Sammuti-ñāṇa because it is included in conventional knowledge by that very generality of dissimilarity.

"Kilesamūlaka" refers to the states of sensual existence rooted in the hindrances (nīvaraṇa).

In the phrase "sā hissa", "assa" refers to that person endowed with the first absorption (paṭhamajjhāna) who is described as "one who is dispassionate towards sensual pleasures." By the word "sveva", while taking the person endowed with the first absorption at the moment of developing dispassion towards sensual pleasures, it is said "being one who is dispassionate towards sensual pleasures" to show the subsequent state of that person after that first absorption. The wisdom of the fourth path is said to penetrate the sixth supernormal power because it attains the state of the sixth supernormal power (āsavakkhaya). Other path-wisdoms are said to penetrate it because they are the strong dependence for that supernormal power. Alternatively, the wisdom in all four paths should be understood as penetrating the sixth supernormal power because of the destruction of taints (āsava) as appropriate, or because of producing that fruit when the destruction of taints, which is the fruit, occurs.

"Kāmasahagata" means having the object of physical sensuality (vatthukāma). "Codenti" means they urge towards sensual pleasures, making the mind incline towards them. "Tadanudhammatā" means simply "tadanudhamma". Since the suffix "tā" has no additional special meaning, it is said "having such a conformable nature." Attachment (nikanti), or the arising of consciousness associated with attachment, is called "wrong mindfulness" (micchāsati). The perceptions and mental applications that take the absorption without initial application as an object, thinking "O, would that the absorption without initial application might arise in me!", are called "accompanied by the absence of initial application" (avitakkasahagata).
205:
It means one who knows directly (abhijānanta) by way of attainment, or one who knows with distinguished knowledge, making manifest that state of the path which is not an object of the absorptions.

An absorption devoid of the five masteries (vasībhāva) is called "unskilled" (appaguṇa). In this Catukka-niddesa, by pointing out the modes of progress and objects of wisdom through the four modes of progress and four objects, wisdom itself is pointed out, and that very wisdom is analyzed in detail.

## The Explanation of the Fourfold Section is finished.

## 5. The Explanation of the Fivefold Section

By the words "fivefold Right Concentration", wisdom is presented as a factor of concentration. Through words such as "pervading with rapture" (pīti-pharaṇatā), that very wisdom is analyzed in detail. The pervading of rapture and happiness should be understood by the method: "That person pervades this very body with rapture and happiness born of seclusion," and so on. Because of establishing the fourth absorption by standing on the object through the pervading of rapture and the pervading of happiness, those wisdoms are said to be "like feet."

In the second fivefold section, by the Pali "concentration with fivefold knowledge", the five knowledges themselves are shown briefly and in detail, with concentration as the heading. The adversaries of mundane concentration, such as the hindrances and attachment to the first absorption, should be suppressed. Other defilements should be restrained. In this concentration of the fruit of Arahantship, however, since all defilements have been subsided, there are no defilements to be suppressed or restrained. Furthermore, it is called "concentration not reached by effort, suppression, or restraint" (na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagato) because it is attained and established without volitional effort at the moment of attainment immediately following the path, or because it is established without decline. By the phrase "due to the state of having reached abundance of mindfulness," it is shown that even when mindfulness is not currently occurring, one is called "mindful" due to the abundance of mindfulness. By the phrase "by way of the delimited time," it is shown that one is called "mindful" by the mindfulness that delimits the time.

## The Explanation of the Fivefold Section is finished.

## 6. Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā
Desiring to show the manifestation of the state of purity, he said: "dūra...pe... rammanāya." By the term "sotadhātuvisuddhi" (purity of the ear-element), the mental states (citta) and mental factors (cetasika) included in the ear-element are taught; therefore, the knowledge (ñāṇa) that is present as the chief among those states is called the knowledge in the purity of the ear-element. It should be understood that this very "cetopariyañāṇa" (knowledge of the penetration of others' minds) is extracted as "paracitte ñāṇa" (knowledge regarding others' minds) according to its meaning. Because the knowledge of passing away and rebirth (cutūpapātañāṇa) is a part of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), it is spoken of as "vaṇṇadhātu-ārammaṇa" (having the element of color/form as its object). It should be understood that by the divine eye knowledge, which is the knowledge of passing away and rebirth that has reached its peak, the whole is called "dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa."

## Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 7. Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā
In the phrase "tadeva ñāṇaṃ," the meaning is that the sixfold knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) is taken together with its status as an object of insight (vipassanā). "Dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇena" means by the knowledge that summarizes the six kinds of knowledge. Indeed, showing the knowledge that occurs in various ways such as "khayadhamma" (subject to destruction) is merely insight into insight (vipassanā-paṭivipassanā), because it shows how to practice insight on preceding knowledges; therefore, the meaning is that that knowledge is not a separate factor (aṅga). However, since the factors are taught everywhere in the Pāḷi text by the word "ñāṇa," the meaning is clear that only the insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) revealed by the word "iti" as "nirodhadhammanti ñāṇaṃ" is the seventh knowledge. Indeed, it is not possible to connect it as "that dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇa is also a single knowledge," because in taking that word "ñāṇa," there is no intention to show the state of knowledge in this dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇa, and because it would lead to having no word to connect with "khayadhamma...pe... nirodhadhamma."

## 10. Dasakaniddesa
## Paṭhamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā
A cause that is not evident is called "aṭṭhāna" (impossible/non-cause), or it is called "aṭṭhāna" because there is no cause. This method is the same for the term "anavakāsa" (no opportunity). The statement "netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati" (this case does not exist) is merely a conclusion of the aforementioned meaning. Perceiving pleasure (sukha) in conditioned things (saṅkhāra) that are not pleasure is only due to the perversion of view (diṭṭhi-vipallāsa). Here, desiring to show the cause of approaching it as pleasure, he spoke of the primary view as "ekanta... by the power of the view of self (attadiṭṭhi)." Making known words that are conducive to a schism in the Saṅgha is called "anussāvana"; or, informing by means of words conducive to a schism in the Saṅgha is "anussāvana."

Even if the gender (linga - female or male) changes, it is only that same continuity of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) produced by a single kamma, and not another; to show this, he said "api parivattalingaṃ." The phrase "ayaṃ pañho" (this is a question) is a statement arising from the desire to know.

The fourfold battle (saṅgāmacatukka) should be applied by way of the enemy soldier. In all cases, the initial intention to kill (abhisandhicitta) is not the criterion for whether it is an ānantariya kamma or not; only the murderous consciousness (vadhakacitta) and the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) which is its object are the criteria for being an ānantariya kamma or not. That gift is given only to a worldling (puthujjana). Why? Just as the murderous consciousness, though having a present object, occurs by taking the interruption of the life-faculty as its object, the volition of generosity (cāga-cetanā) does not occur in that way. That volition of generosity is merely the act of relinquishing, taking the object to be relinquished as its focus; relinquishing it is making it the property of another. Therefore, it is given only to the person for whom it was made their own property.

The statement "saṇṭha... he is released only at the destruction of the aeon (kappa)" does not agree with the Kappa Commentary. In that commentary, it is said: "This sutta 'āpāyiko' is spoken with reference to the life-span aeon (āykappa) where that person, having divided one aeon into eighty parts, would remain for just one part of that time." In the phrase "only at the destruction of the aeon," if the meaning is "only at the destruction of the life-span aeon," there is no contradiction. Here, the word "saṇṭhahante" (remaining/persisting) is spoken by way of imagining what is not there, like saying "it will be destroyed tomorrow." He is cooked in hell for only one day; after that, since there is no aeon, there is also no life-span aeon. Thus, the connection of meaning should be understood as non-contradictory.

"Pakatatta" means a monk who has not been expelled (from the Saṅgha). "Samānasaṃvāsaka" means a monk who has not committed a Pārājika offense.
208:
The meaning is: what dhamma makes that person, who is called 'fixed' (niyata), fixed? The state of being a fixed person as questioned does not exist by its own nature, like the states of fixed wrongness (micchatta-niyata) or fixed rightness (sammatta-niyata). Rejecting the cause of being fixed as questioned, [the teacher] said, 'By the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha...' and so on, to show the intended cause by which one is called 'fixed' or 'one with seven lives at most' (sattakkhattuparama) due to the insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) for the three higher paths.

Just as a name is given to a newborn boy, for a Sotāpanna born into the Noble birth (ariya-jāti), terms like 'niyata' and 'sattakkhattuparama' are merely names. It means it is a name distinguished by being fixed or not fixed.

If a prior cause (pubba-hetu) were the fixing factor, the Sotāpanna would be a fixed person. Because of the state of being a decisive support (upanissaya) for the three higher paths from the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), there is the function of the prior cause. However, before that Path of Stream-entry, there is no function of a prior cause, and thus it would lead to the fault that there is no decisive support for the Path of Stream-entry. If there were a prior cause as a decisive support for that Path of Stream-entry as well, and if that were the fixing factor, one would be fixed even before the arising of the Path of Stream-entry. That is undesirable. Therefore, regarding the meaning that it would lead to being without cause through the prior cause of this Path of Stream-entry, it was said: 'Thus, this person reaches an arising that is without cause and without condition.'

The path obtained is the Path of Stream-entry. When there is the fixing of 'seven lives at most' and so on because of that Path of Stream-entry, the defilements (kilesa) which are the root of suffering that would occur beyond the seventh birth are exhausted by that very path. Therefore, it means the three higher paths are without further function (needless). If the three higher paths were to fix the 'seven lives at most' and so on, then there would be no other Sotāpanna besides that, leading to the meaning that the Path of Stream-entry is without function or purpose. Alternatively, the function of seeing is the abandoning of self-identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) and so on. Due to the abandoning of those, the state of 'seven lives at most' and so on should occur. And that occurs only through the higher paths. Therefore, because of the continuous occurrence of results beyond the seventh birth, if there is insight that emerges from the formations (saṅkhāra) without that Path of Stream-entry, the abandoning of self-identity view and so on would occur without that Path of Stream-entry. Therefore, it was said: 'The defilements should be exhausted without having arisen through the first path.' The phrase 'no one else fixes it' means there is no other fixing factor besides insight (vipassanā), which is the cause for giving the name. The statement that 'only insight fixes it' is also said with reference only to the cause for giving the name. Therefore, it was said: 'Thus, it is merely a name given by the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.'

There is the meaning 'they do not arise'. The Blessed One, standing in this world-system and saying, 'I have no teacher, no one like me exists,' and so on...
209:
"Friend Sāriputta, if I were asked whether there are other ascetics or brahmins who realize the Four Noble Truths equally with the Blessed One at this time, I would say, 'No, venerable sir.'" Having said this, to show the reason for being able to answer thus, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, showed this sutta: "It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Worthy Ones, Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, should arise simultaneously in a single world-system." This means that, excluding this world-system which is the Buddha-field (buddha-khetta), another Buddha cannot arise elsewhere [within it].

The training rules (sikkhāpada) taught with the words "Whichever monk..." and so on are called the Mātikā. When that Mātikā disappears, the Dispensation (Sāsana) stands in the Pātimokkha, known as the recitation of the introduction (nidānuddesa), and in the acts of novice ordination (pabbajjā) and higher ordination (upasampadā). Alternatively, novice ordination and higher ordination are included within the Pātimokkha; since there can be no Pātimokkha without both of them, it is said that the Dispensation stands in the Pātimokkha and in those [ordinations]. "Receded" (osakkita) means taking the two—the final penetration of the Four Noble Truths and the final breaking of virtue—together, after which the Dispensation is said to be destroyed. "Tā" refers to the rays of light. "Kāruñña" refers to the pitiable state of lamentation.

"Because there is no wonder" means because of the fault of lacking the quality of being a wonder if two Buddhas were to arise. "So that there is no dispute" means two Buddhas do not arise simultaneously in order to prevent disputes.

Because it bears only one Buddha, it is called "Eka-buddha-dhāraṇီ" (the one-Buddha-bearer). By this, it is shown that the qualities of the Buddhas are of such a nature that this world-system is unable to bear the qualities of a second Buddha. For it is not possible to bear the special nature of dhammas produced by special causes [perfections]. Because it can move evenly on the surface of the water, it is called "Samupādikā", meaning one who moves evenly on the water. "Of both" means both Buddhas, or the weight of the bodies of both Buddhas. "Covering" means making it pleasing. "With just one meal" means one would die after swallowing just one morsel of food.

"By the excessive weight of the Dhamma" means: since the earth stands because of the Dhamma, why does it shake because of that very Dhamma? Again, the Elder Nāgasena said: "In the world, a treasure that supports a household and is highly desired by people is seen to be an excessive weight that causes a cart to break because of its own heavy nature. Similarly, although the Dhamma is highly desired by the wise because it supports those possessed of it with special benefits and happiness, it becomes an excessive weight and the cause of the earth shaking because of its heavy nature due to its profound and immeasurable state."

Venerable Nāgasena spoke the words "a cart" and so on. It means it is brought in and carried from another cart. "Natural" means it is not a nature caused by shouting (not an artificial nature). Because the qualities of a Buddha arise due to many causes of perfections, it is said that "only one Buddha arises in the world." Just as things like the earth are great and exist as only one in their own sphere, similarly, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha is great and is the only one in His own sphere. What is the sphere of that Blessed One? Whatever knowable things (ñeyya-dhamma) exist to whatever extent, that is the sphere of the Buddha. Thus, it is said that the Blessed One, whose sphere is infinite like the sky, is the only one.
210:
To show the meaning that the wise consider [the Dhamma] to be very heavy because of its profound and incomparable nature, and its weightiness, which causes the earth to shake, the Elder Nāgasena said: "Great King, in this world, there are two carts..." and so on. "Ekassa" means from one cart, or taking the treasure of one cart from that cart. "Osāritaṃ" means brought in, conveyed, or spoken.

"Sabhāvapakatikā" means not having a nature produced by proclamation (or not having an artificial nature). "Kāraṇamahantattā" means that the qualities of the Buddha arise because of the greatness of the causes, namely the perfections (pāramīs). Just as the earth and other great elements are unique each in their own domain, so too the Sammāsambuddha is unique in His own domain. What is the domain of that Blessed One? As far as the extent of the knowable (ñeyya) reaches, so far is His domain. Thus, the Blessed One, who has an infinite domain like the sky, is unique; by saying this, the Elder Nāgasena shows that there is no second Buddha even in other world systems.

In the preliminary stage before the action, the "endowment of striving" (āyūhana-samangitā) should be understood through the power of exertion, and the "endowment of volition" (cetanā-samangitā) through the power of the decisive volition. Or, it should be understood in connection with the moment of the mental continuum performing the action. The word "vipākārahaṃ" (worthy of result) is spoken with reference to the nature of ripening in the second life and so forth. "Calati" means it changes (parivattati). A hunter who habitually travels with dogs is called "sunakhavājika".

## The Explanation of the First Description of Powers (Pathama-bala-niddesa) is finished.

## The Explanation of the Second Description of Powers (Dutiya-bala-niddesa)

To show that there is no other achievement of destination (gati-sampatti) apart from the state of existence reached, he said: "The destination is achieved" (sampannā gati). The time of good kings such as Mahāsudassana, and the time of good humans such as the first inhabitants of the world-cycle, is called achievement of time (kāla-sampatti).

Regarding the statement "Indeed, there is only an opportunity for the wholesome," if some enemy should oppress a person established in the achievement of effort (payoga-sampatti) such as good bodily conduct, such oppression occurs only because of the distorted view born of causes like the enemy's envy. That achievement of effort is, by its nature, only a cause for a pleasant result and not a cause for a painful result; this is the intended meaning. Just as a monkey does not know how to untie and eat a bundle of rice at the place where it is tied, but breaks and destroys it anywhere, so too one who is unskilled in means destroys wealth. By the words "discarding in a cemetery" and so on, he shows that just as a corpse killed and discarded cannot rise again, there is no rising up from the states of deprivation (apāya).
211:
"Paccari" is also the name of a raft; because it was compiled on that raft, this commentary is called "Mahāpaccari". Why is it said that "death in the water and death on land are the same," when Sakka, the King of Devas, had said, "I will protect the Elder Samuddarakkhita"? It is true that he said so, but the Elders said this to clearly show the nature of life as being quickly changeable (easily subject to death). The meaning is: "Because it is quickly changeable, I will not go for the sake of life." Alternatively, "in the water" refers to Nagadīpa, and "on land" refers to Jambudīpa.

"The Elder does not give" means he did not give because he thought, "How does this lay devotee know me? Could someone have told him something?" That is why he said, "We also do not know." "Of another monk" should be connected as: "Taking the bowl of another monk... he placed it in the hand of the Elder." "Anāyatanē" means in a place of destruction that is without cause or improper. The meaning is: "You should protect yourself; as for us, we are old and infirm, what could we do even if we protected ourselves? Being old and infirm, we will not be able to protect ourselves." Or, because the Elder was an Anāgāmi (Non-returner), he knew what he should say and gave the exhortation.

"Sammāpayogassa gatamaggo" means the cause for knowing that practice, because it was accomplished through right effort (sammā-payoga).

It means that he will state an unreal simile by making use of a real meaning. "Manussā" (Humans) refers to people appointed to jobs such as treasurers; they were unable to receive it because of its greatness.

## The Explanation of the Second Description of Powers (Dutiya-bala-niddesa) is finished.

## The Explanation of the Third Description of Powers (Tatiya-bala-niddesa)

"Añcitā" means gone or arisen. "Peccā" means again, or after death. "Ussannattā" is said to be due to an excess of thought (vitakka) or due to an abundance of courage and so on. "Dibbanti" means they sport and play.

There are eight Great Hells: Sañjီva, Kālasutta, Saṅghāta, Roruva, Mahāroruva, Tapana, Mahātapana, and Avīci. In each one, there are four gates, and at each gate, there are four Ussada hells such as the Hell of Filth (Gūtha-niraya); thus, they describe sixteen Ussada hells.
212:
The chief celestial king, like Sakka, Suyama, and others, as well as the attendant who performs the second and subsequent ranks of office, like Pajāpati, Varuṇa, Īsāna, and others, will arise.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Third Power is finished.

## The Description of the Fourth Power
'Kappa' means having a twofold end (having two different ends). In this description of the fourth power, the diversity of the aggregates (khandha) and other elements should be understood through the power of the diversity of elements such as seeds and so forth.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Fourth Power is finished.

## The Description of the Fifth Power
'Ajjhāsayadhātu' (the element of disposition) refers to the nature of disposition (ajjhāsaya). Just as the elemental nature of things like excrement (gūtha) and so forth associates only with excrement and so forth, so too the nature of the disposition of persons means that those who are immoral (dussīla) and so forth associate only with those who are immoral and so forth. The monks also said to one another, "Friends, these people, saying 'Enjoy according to your own nature,' know our similarity or dissimilarity, distinguish between those of low disposition and those of noble disposition, and then, wishing to see the application of that disposition, they lead us into actions connected with that element." Thus, because of the discernment of the element of disposition only by the power of similarity, it is meant that it is determined according to the similarity of the element of disposition.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Fifth Power is finished.

## The Description of the Sixth Power
In this (Ñāṇavibhaṅga Pāḷi), 'carita' (conduct) refers to misconduct and good conduct. Because those beings have the eye of wisdom with little dust (of lust, hatred, and delusion), the meaning is clarified as 'apparajakkha' (those with little dust in their eyes). The meaning of the word can also be 'apparajakkha' because there is little dust in the eye of wisdom of those beings. In this (description of the sixth power), by knowing the disposition and so forth...
213:
It should be understood that it clarifies the knowledge of those faculties, whether superior or inferior, by which beings have good or bad dispositions and so forth. By doing so, the distinctness and uniqueness of the 'Knowledge of the Higher and Lower Faculties' (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) and the 'Knowledge of Dispositions and Latent Tendencies' (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) are established, as well as the distinctness of the 'Knowledge of the Higher and Lower Faculties' and the 'Knowledge of Diverse Inclinations' (nānādhimuttika-ñāṇa) as powers (bala).

'Yadariyā' means those who are Noble Ones (ariya). 'Āvasiṃsu' means they lived depending on [certain abodes]. Who are those Noble Ones? "Monks, in this Dispensation, a monk is one who has abandoned five factors, is endowed with six factors, has a single guard, has four supports, has discarded individual truths, has well-relinquished searches, has pure thoughts, has calmed bodily formations, has a well-liberated mind, and has well-liberated wisdom." Thus it was spoken. Among those ten, the abandoning of the five factors, the discarding of individual truths, and the well-relinquishing of searches, as well as the 'dispelling' among the four supports spoken of as "reflecting with wisdom, he uses some, endures some, avoids some, and dispels some," are only the functions of the Path (magga); the remaining abodes of the Noble Ones (ariyāvāsa) are also accomplished only by the Path. Therefore, it was said, "This sutta... shows."

Between the latent tendency in the object and the latent tendency in the continuity, one lies latent in a pleasant object (iṭṭhārammaṇa) by way of the latent tendency in the object. By the phrase 'āciṇṇasamāciṇṇā,' it shows the state of lying latent by way of being established as if wrapped around from all sides. Because existence (bhava) is also an object of craving (vatthukāma), or because it is similar by the power of lust (rāga), it was said, "The latent tendency of lust for existence... is included."

"Those with noble inclinations (adhimutti) are those with sharp faculties; the others are those with dull faculties." Thus, the taking of 'inclination' is only for the purpose of showing the distinction of the faculties. Therefore, it was said, "For the purpose of showing the state of sharp faculties and dull faculties."

In the phrase 'by the power of the order of abandonment,' the order of abandonment should be understood as the order of the things to be abandoned and the person who abandons. Alternatively, whichever dhamma is to be abandoned, that dhamma is spoken of first by that abandonment; after that, the dhamma not to be abandoned is spoken of. This is the order of abandonment.

The faculties that are the strong dependence (upanissaya) for the Path are called 'upanissaya-indriya.'

Because of the lack of desire for peace (Nibbāna), they have entered the 'state of lack of desire' (acchandikaṭṭhāna). When a certain life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is occurring, the supramundane (lokuttara) arises in that continuity; that life-continuum is the basis for that supramundane [mind].

## The Explanation of the Description of the Sixth Power is finished.
